newsitem.title: POLAND: Gdansk shipyard crisis prompts more protests.
newsitem.headline: Gdansk shipyard crisis prompts more protests.

text.p: Almost 2,000 workers from the bankrupt Gdansk shipyard blocked roads and trams in the Baltic coast city on Wednesday, while in Warsaw the Solidarity union launched plans for nationwide protests.

The demonstrators set alight tyres and paint barrels at a crucial crossroads in protest at losing their jobs, sending ominous plumes of dark smoke over Gdansk while traffic jams stretched for many kilometres (miles) out of the city centre.

The yard's receiver announced last week that he would have to sack the remaining 3,800 workers at the yard which gave birth to the Solidarity trade union in 1980, and sell its assets off piecemeal rather than as a going concern.

In Warsaw, Solidarity's National Committee announced that by Monday midnight it would have a plan ready for a nationwide campaign against the ex-communist-led government's policy towards the yard and other embattled industries such as arms.
"The effects of this action will be felt by everyone," union spokesman Piotr Zak told reporters.
He said the campaign could involved demonstrations and strikes, but details would only be settled next week.
Asked whether the union was seeking negotiations, its national chief Marian Krzaklewski said the government had previously sapped workers' determination by offering talks.
"This is not an invitation to talks but to action. We don't want talks just to chat," he said.
The government has refused to subsidise the 60-percent state treasury-owned shipyard which was declared bankrupt last year with debts of 415 million zlotys ($136 million).
The government did offer partial loan guarantees, only if a bank lent it money to keep going until an investor emerged.
Polish bank Pekao SA prompted the receiver's decision to shut up shop last week by refusing a $100 million loan for construction of five ships for a German shipowner.
At a rally by the shipyard gates just before Wednesday's protest, the yard's deputy Solidarity chief angrily accused the left-dominated government of having aroused false hopes.
"The Communists have cheated us," said Karol Guzikiewicz.
"We have been guilty of one mistake -- we naively believed the communists when they said they wanted to save our shipyard," he said.
The yard workers, whose Wednesday action lasted one hour, said they aimed to block Gdansk's railways on Thursday.
Krzaklewski said in Warsaw that he had applied for official permission to raise funds for saving the shipyard through the sale of contribution coupons.
Solidarity hopes that if it can obtain 50 million zlotys ($16.6 million) in this way it can find an investor ready to add 100 million ($33.2 million) more to build ships.
Solidarity, which toppled communism in 1989, says the leftist coalition government has refused to help the yard because of its opposition links.
Solidarity has grouped rightist opposition parties in an alliance which is leading opinion polls and could beat the coalition at parliamentary polls due in September this year.

Even if Solidarity wins, the victory would come too late for the Gdansk shipyard, where Lech Walesa founded Solidarity as the Soviet bloc's first free union -- which went on to play a key role in toppling communist rule in 1989.
